title: Berkshire 1988 letter: arbitrage, permanent holdings, owner-managers and why CEOs go unmeasured
summary: Buffett reports a 20% gain in 1988 and explains why a growing capital base is Berkshire's main problem. He covers buying Borsheim's on a handshake, holding wonderful businesses forever, how he approaches arbitrage, and why efficient market theory fails. He also explains why GAAP is only a starting point and why CEOs escape the accountability faced by subordinates.

principles.text: A growing capital base is the main drag on returns; compounding gets harder each year.
principles.quote: The major problem we face, however, is a growing capital base. You’ve heard that from us before, but this problem, like age, grows in significance each year.

principles.text: With outstanding businesses and managers, the favorite holding period is forever.
principles.quote: In fact, when we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever.

principles.text: Concentrate in a few companies you understand well and hold strong long-term convictions about.
principles.quote: We continue to concentrate our investments in a very few companies that we try to understand well. There are only a handful of businesses about which we have strong long-term convictions.

principles.text: CEOs escape the accountability that subordinates face: fuzzy standards, unmeasured boards, taboo criticism.
principles.quote: The supreme irony of business management is that it is far easier for an inadequate CEO to keep his job than it is for an inadequate subordinate.

principles.text: Never forecast the market, rates or the economy; invest on long-term business prospects of specific companies.
principles.quote: We do not have, never have had, and never will have an opinion about where the stock market, interest rates, or business activity will be a year from now.

principles.text: Efficient market theory is wrong because the market is often, not always, efficient; superior returns come from facts and discipline.
principles.quote: Observing correctly that the market was frequently efficient, they went on to conclude incorrectly that it was always efficient. The difference between these propositions is night and day.
